findings.title: Blocked-email lookup is case-sensitive and unnormalized
findings.body: BlockedEmail.should_block? looks up the address with an exact BlockedEmail.where(email: email) match, and neither this method nor EmailValidator downcases or strips the value first. PostgreSQL's unique index is also case-sensitive, so a row stored as "bad@spam.com" will not match a signup of "Bad@spam.com" or " bad@spam.com". The block is therefore bypassed by trivial casing or whitespace changes, and the new blocked-email control does not actually stop the address it was meant to stop.

findings.title: Domain allow/deny regex is unanchored
findings.body: email_in_restriction_setting? builds Regexp.new("@(#{domains})") and tests it with =~, with no end anchor and with only "." escaped. A blacklist entry of "gmail.com" therefore matches "user@gmail.com.evil.test" as well as the real domain, and a whitelist entry likewise treats that host as allowed. Attackers can evade the domain blacklist (and pass a whitelist) by appending another label, so the restriction this validator is supposed to enforce does not hold.

findings.title: Block check writes stats and is counted twice per signup
findings.body: should_block? increments match_count and saves last_match_at as a side effect of validation, using a non-atomic read-modify-write. UsersController#create calls user.valid? and then user.save, and save validates again, so one signup attempt runs EmailValidator twice and advances match_count by 2. Concurrent attempts can also lose updates. last_match_at and match_count therefore do not record how many times the address was actually submitted, which breaks the statistic this table is added to track.
